prayer.text: North American Martyrs, pray for us.

cues.text: Blackrobes in a New World

Beginning in the 1620s and 1630s, French Jesuit missionaries — known to New France’s indigenous peoples as Blackrobes for their distinctive habit — established missions among the Huron around Georgian Bay.
They labored for years to learn difficult indigenous languages, adapt to an unfamiliar way of life, and win converts amid a culture still largely committed to its traditional religious practices.
Among these missionaries, Jean de Brébeuf was a Norman priest whose poor health as a young novice worried his superiors.
They doubted he could sustain missionary life’s physical demands, yet he became the Huron mission’s most experienced and respected voice, laboring there on and off for over two decades.
Isaac Jogues, Captured and Mutilated
In 1642, Isaac Jogues , a gifted young priest and former professor of literature, was captured alongside the lay missionary René Goupil by Iroquois raiders while returning to the mission from Quebec.
Goupil was killed almost immediately, reportedly for making the sign of the cross over a child.
He became the first of the group to die.
Jogues himself endured over a year of brutal captivity and slave labor, during which several of his fingers were bitten off or mutilated by his captors.
Jogues eventually escaped with the help of Dutch traders and returned to France, where he was received with astonishment by a court and Church that had assumed him dead.

Pope Urban VIII reportedly granted him special permission to celebrate Mass despite his mutilated hands, remarking that it would be shameful for a martyr of Christ not to be allowed to drink the Blood of Christ.

Remarkably, Jogues chose to return to the same dangerous mission field, where he was killed by tomahawk blows at Ossernenon in October 1646, in the very territory of the people who had once enslaved him.
Brébeuf's Long Martyrdom
The gravest crisis struck in March 1649, when Iroquois forces invaded Huronia in overwhelming numbers, destroying village after village.
Brébeuf and his younger companion Gabriel Lalemant were captured near the mission of Saint-Ignace and subjected to prolonged, deliberate torture.
This included burning, mutilation, and mockery of the sacraments they had come to teach.

Brébeuf endured it for several hours with such remarkable composure that, tradition holds, his executioners drank his blood and ate his heart afterward, hoping to absorb some measure of the courage they had witnessed.
The Remaining Martyrs
The wider Iroquois campaign against Huronia claimed the rest of the group across these same years.
Anthony Daniel was killed defending his mission chapel at Teanaustaye in 1648.
Charles Garnier was shot while ministering to the dying amid a burning village in 1649.
Noël Chabanel was killed the same year while attempting to reach a place of safety.
The lay missionary Jean de Lalande was killed alongside Isaac Jogues in 1646 while attempting to defend him.
A Mission That Survived Its Missionaries
The destruction of the Huron missions and the deaths of these eight men marked a devastating short-term setback for the young Church in New France.
Yet the faith these missionaries had planted did not disappear with them.

Scattered by the Iroquois invasion, Huron Christian communities carried elements of that faith into subsequent generations, while the martyrs' sacrifice took deep and lasting root in the wider Canadian and American Catholic Church's devotional life.
Legacy
Canonized together in 1930 by Pope Pius XI as the North American Martyrs , these eight men included six priests and two lay missionaries.
They are honored today at national shrines in both Midland, Ontario, and Auriesville, New York, drawing pilgrims to the very ground where they lived and died.
Their combined witness remains a permanent testimony to missionary courage that counted no hardship, however extreme, too great a price.
It carried the Gospel into a genuinely unknown and often dangerous world—a sacrifice offered, in every case, not in bitterness toward the peoples who killed them, but in hope.
That hope outlasted their own mortal lives by centuries.
